newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crudes muted by London Easter holiday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crudes muted by London Easter holiday.

text.p: The Easter holiday in London kept the U.S. foreign crude scene muted on Monday as traders waited for their transatlantic counterparts to return on Tuesday.
Limited talk continued to focus on whether Swiss trader Glencore would bring a fixed ULCC of North Sea Brent to the Gulf Coast or South Africa.
Gulf Coast bids for the cargoes were around May WTI minus 90 cents a barrel for late-April arrival.
One potential buyer said the price might be attractive enough to justify buying for storage in the Caribbean.

The May spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent was around $1.20-25 a barrel Monday afternoon. This narrow level would ordinarily discourage transatlantic trade if not for the weakness of dated Brent, which stood around May Brent minus 85 cents, traders said.
One U.S.-based trader said there were plenty of sweet North Sea barrels available, including talk surrounding Gullfaks and Oseberg.
Nigerian crudes such as Qua Iboe were also heard to be plentiful, although heavy sweets such as Cabinda were "cleaned up" for the moment.
Sweet domestic cash grade differentials were talked slightly weaker Monday, reflecting the resolution of civil unrest in Nigeria.
Last week's disturbances shut down some 210,000 barrel per day (bpd) of Nigerian production from top equity producer Royal Dutch/Shell's operations, or about 10 percent of the country's total flows.
Shell said Monday it was restarting oil output at all affected locations following the restoration of peace in the region.
The shutdown prompted the Anglo-Dutch oil giant to declare force majeur on four cargoes of Forcados loading in early April, delaying the shipments by three days. No export shipments were cancelled.
Sour crudes, such as Colombian Cano Limon, Ecuadoran Oriente as well as long-haul grades such as Iraqi Basrah Light, remain ample.
On the Latin American front, Colombia's Vasconia and Cano Limon were pegged at WTI minus $3.70 and $3.25 a barrel, respectively.
